\chapter{You're Welcome}
\label{ch:ar-youre-welcome}
\hlchaptermodality{23}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can reply to shukran with ʿafwan, and use the same word to say excuse me.}

Say ʿafwan as the reply to thanks, unpack the root 'to erase' behind it, and hear the same -an ending it shares with shukran.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ar{عفوا}]{\ar{عفوا} (ʿafwan) — \textquotedblleft{}you're welcome,\textquotedblright{} from a root meaning \textquotedblleft{}to erase\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:AR-C23-afwan}



\begin{quote}
Your very first Arabic lesson already used this word once, in passing, as the reply to \emph{shukran}. Here it gets its own full treatment — starting with a root that literally means \textquotedblleft{}to erase.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ar{عفوا}} (\emph{ʿafwan}), root \textbf{ʿ-f-w} (\textbf{\ar{ع}-\ar{ف}-\ar{و}}): the root's core sense is \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to erase, obliterate, remove}\textquotedblright{} — and \textquotedblleft{}to pardon, forgive\textquotedblright{} grows directly out of that, since forgiving something is, metaphorically, \textbf{erasing} it. The same root gives \textbf{\ar{العفو}} (\emph{al-ʿAfuww}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the Supreme Pardoner}\textquotedblright{}), one of the \textbf{99 names of Allah} in Islamic tradition.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest: ʿafwan does more than one job}
\textbf{ʿAfwan} answers \emph{shukran} as \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{you're welcome}\textquotedblright{} — but depending on tone and context, the exact same word also does duty as \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{excuse me},\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{pardon},\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{sorry}.\textquotedblright{} One root, one word, several closely related jobs — all growing from that same \textquotedblleft{}erase/pardon\textquotedblright{} sense.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same ending as shukran itself}]
Look closely at the spelling: \textbf{\ar{عفوا}} ends in the same \textbf{tanwīn fatḥ} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{-an}\textquotedblright{}) you already met in \textbf{\ar{شكرا}} (\emph{shukran}) — the indefinite accusative ending. Neither word is a full sentence with its own verb; both are fixed, idiomatic accusative forms functioning as a complete conversational turn on their own. The grammar you learned once, for \emph{shukran}, already explains \emph{ʿafwan} too.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\ar{عفوا}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ʿafwan}, \textquotedblleft{}you're welcome\textquotedblright{}
  \item the root ʿ-f-w — \textquotedblleft{}to erase\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}to pardon\textquotedblright{}
  \item the shared ending — shukran and ʿafwan both end in the same tanwīn fatḥ, \textquotedblleft{}-an\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the root \textbf{ʿ-f-w} literally mean, before it comes to mean \textquotedblleft{}pardon\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}To erase, obliterate.\textquotedblright{}}) Besides \textquotedblleft{}you're welcome,\textquotedblright{} what other jobs can \textbf{ʿafwan} do? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}Excuse me,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}pardon,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{}} — context-dependent.) What grammatical ending does \emph{ʿafwan} share with \emph{shukran}? (The \textbf{tanwīn fatḥ}, \textquotedblleft{}-an\textquotedblright{} — both are fixed indefinite- accusative forms, not full sentences.)
\end{tcolorbox}
